name: Proper Name in a Descriptive NP
pattern: NP[Determiner + Nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified]

entry.name: Proper Name in a Descriptive NP
entry.pattern: NP[Determiner + Nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified]

1.definition: Counts or distinguishes bearers of the same name.
1.details: In two Kims, two individuals satisfy the description ‘has the name Kim’. A modifier can select one Kim from that group. This use can be created even if Kim has never previously been used as an ordinary count noun in that community.

examples.form: There are [two Kims] on the committee.

2.definition: Describes a person by resemblance to a salient bearer of the name.
2.details: In another Einstein, the person evaluated need not have the name Einstein. A name can contribute properties of the bearer, selected by the context. With no Einstein the interpretation concerns the absence of those properties.

examples.form: They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

3.definition: Selects a manifestation, product, or copy associated with the named entity.
3.details: The Paris of her youth identifies a period or version of Paris. A Rembrandt can refer to a painting. Some Beethoven can refer to music. A copy of a publication can be described by the title with a possessive determiner.

examples.note: Constructed example with count syntax and an artwork interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The descriptive NP is built around a form otherwise used as a name.
A strong proper name independently supplies a definite referent without a determiner.
An introduction can establish which entity a form names. Secondary constructions can then use a standing name descriptively.

grounds.note: Documents name-bearer and resemblance uses and leaves the number of constructions open.
Distinguishes name bearers, resemblance, manifestations, products and copies.

projection.target: Numeral and plural marking can count bearers, and an indefinite NP can describe resemblance, including when the described person has a different name. Product uses independently admit count and non-count construals.
projection.evidence: FrameNet supplies name-bearer and resemblance uses of the same form family. CGEL documents those readings along with manifestations, products and copies. Their differing entailments motivate keeping the readings visible while leaving the number of constructions open.

curious.title: Names used like ordinary nouns
curious.summary: A name can be counted, compared with, or used to mean something connected to the named person or place.
curious.body: In There are two Kims on the committee, Kim is used to count people who share a name. In They were hoping to recruit another Einstein, the person wanted needn't be called Einstein; what's meant is someone with the relevant qualities of Einstein. A name can also pick out a version of something, a product or a copy: They bought a Rembrandt can mean they bought a painting, and some Beethoven can mean music. This dictionary keeps these readings visible without saying how many separate constructions they are, and marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.
They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

curious.try: Can you think of a name that stands for a type of person, such as someone known for a quality? How would you say you wanted another one?

teacher.summary: Explains how names can behave like count nouns with number, determiners and modifiers.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a NP with a determiner and a nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified. This dictionary distinguishes readings: counting or distinguishing bearers of the same name (two Kims, where a modifier can select one Kim), resemblance (another Einstein, where the person needn't have that name), and a manifestation, product or copy associated with the named entity (a Rembrandt, some Beethoven, the Paris of her youth). Numeral and plural marking can count bearers, and an indefinite NP can describe resemblance. Product uses admit count and non-count construals. This dictionary leaves open how many constructions there are. It's marked provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary describes these as proper names in descriptive NPs.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.
They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

watch_for: A learner might expect another Einstein to mean a person called Einstein, when the person need not have that name.
A learner might think a Rembrandt refers to the painter.
A learner might think a name cannot take a determiner or a plural ending.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences using names in descriptive NPs into three groups (same name, resembles, product or copy) and justify their choices.

child.hook: What do you call it when two kids are both named Kim?
child.explain: A name can be counted. If two people are named Kim, we can say two Kims.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.

child.play: Think of a name shared by two people you know. Count them aloud, then say a sentence about each one.
